newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US says Iraqi oil could already be flowing.
newsitem.headline: US says Iraqi oil could already be flowing.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday that if Iraq had not sent its troops into the Kurdish north the oil-for-food deal could have been implemented in early September.
Edward Gnehm, the deputy U.S. ambassador, made the comment in reply to a to General Assembly speech from Iraq's foreign minister Mohammad al-Sahaf.
"The truth is that the secretariat of the United Nations had informed Iraq in late August that implementation of (U.N. Resolution) 986 could begin in the first week of September."

It was the first official confirmation that the oil deal had been that close to implementation. But Gnehm said Iraqi forces launched a military action against the Kurdish city of Arbil causing a rapid deterioration in the security situation in northern Iraq.

"Let this be clear ... by today's date, oil could well have been flowing and humanitarian goods already delivered under terms of 986 if not for the action Iraq took in August 31. That is the only reason for the current delay in implementing the resolution" that sets out terms for the oil-for-food place," he added.
"We look forward to the time that the questions raised by Iraq's reckless actions in the north can be resolved and the resolution at last implemented," he said."

Gnehm also said that "Since President Saddam Hussein himself has never uttered the word 986 publicly and has never publicly endorsed (the resolution's) implementation, we assume he remains opposed to it as he always has been.

"We are disappointed that we did not hear from the foreign minister that he would stop punishing the secretary-general, who was again attacked viciously in the Iraqi press today, to change the administrative arrangements the secretariat has already prepared in order to implement 986," Gnehm said.

He was referring to an article in Babel, the newspaper owned by Saddam Hussein's son, Uday, which accused U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali of delaying the oil-for-food deal because he wanted to please the United States and further his chances for re-election.
Washington has said it would veto a second five-year term for Boutros-Ghali and would not change its mind on the subject.
